query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous wear and corrosive attack, high-entropy alloys resist degradation because mechanical deformation continuously exposes fresh reactive sites that trigger rapid formation of a self-healing, passivating oxide layer. This film, regenerated by the alloy's reactive elements (such as Cr, Al, or Ti), acts as a dynamic barrier to both mechanical wear and chemical corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure that includes reactive elements prone to forming stable oxides.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled environment where it experiences continuous mechanical abrasion in a corrosive medium (e.g., saline solution), while another set of samples is tested under isolated wear or isolated corrosion conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at specified loads, speeds, and temperatures in a corrosive medium; comparisons are made to baseline tests with only wear or only corrosion to isolate synergistic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: A deformation-induced passivating oxide film that continuously regenerates on the alloy’s surface as wear exposes fresh metal.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical abrasion generates new surfaces that rapidly oxidize due to the presence of reactive elements, forming a protective film. The film acts as a barrier to both mechanical damage and corrosive agents, thereby reducing overall material loss. The cyclic removal and reformation of the film under stress creates a synergy that enhances durability against both degradation modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined degradation, the alloy will show lower overall material loss and evidence of a continuously regenerating protective film compared to the baseline tests (isolated wear or corrosion), where such a film either does not form or does not regenerate rapidly enough.
generation.baseline: In isolated wear or corrosion tests on similar alloys lacking the reactive element enrichment, there is a higher rate of material loss due to the absence (or slower formation) of a protective oxide film.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds when the mechanical abrasion is sufficient to promote film renewal without overwhelming the film formation kinetics. It may fail if the abrasive force is too high (exceeding the film’s ability to reform) or if the corrosive aggressiveness is such that it chemically disrupts the film faster than it can form.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the film’s formation and its durability under varying rates of wear and corrosion are not fully determined, and may depend on local environmental factors and alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one enriched with reactive elements (e.g., Cr, Al, or Ti) expected to form the protective oxide, and one with similar mechanical properties but with lower levels of such elements. Subject both sets to a simultaneous corrosive and wear environment under identical controlled conditions.
measurements: Surface film thickness and continuity via high-resolution microscopy
Wear track morphology and evidence of oxide reformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enriched alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in overall degradation (combined wear and corrosion) and fails to display evidence of a regenerating passivating film compared to the control alloy, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

frame.system: High‐entropy alloys (HEAs) that are engineered via multi‐principal (often near‐equimolar) compositions to form complex, micro‐structurally stable phases with the propensity to develop protective passive oxide films in service. The starting state is an alloy with a well‐defined, homogeneous or nano‐structured distribution of elements typical of available HEAs.
frame.goal: To develop and validate a single unifying mechanistic hypothesis that explains how the integrity and self-healing behavior of passive oxide films govern the resistance to simultaneous mechanical wear and chemical corrosion in HEAs.
frame.limitation: The lack of a clear mechanistic understanding linking the behavior of protective passive films under mechanical abrasion to their performance in corrosive media, i.e., why the synergy between wear and corrosion resistance exists and how it can be predicted.
constraints: The hypothesis must be singular and mechanistic in nature.
A controlled comparison with a well-matched baseline (for example, an HEA variant with a slightly modified composition expected to alter oxide film stability) is required.
The experimental design should separately quantify and distinguish the contributions of wear and corrosion, as well as their synergistic effects.
frame.regime: Testing should be performed under combined mechanical stress (e.g., standardized sliding or abrasion tests) within corrosive environments (e.g., saline or acidic electrolytes) at controlled temperatures and loads that mimic service conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have typically focused on wear resistance and corrosion resistance separately, often attributing performance improvements to either the formation of stable oxide films or the inherent mechanical hardness. However, these approaches fell short in explaining the interactive phenomena observed in simultaneous degradation, as the methodologies did not allow for decoupling or correlating the performance of the protective film under mechanical perturbation.

families.principle: Isolating specific variables in a controlled setting to establish a direct causal link between a hypothesized mechanism and observed integrated degradation (wear–corrosion) outcomes.
cues_against: No explicit cues for relying solely on observational techniques
families.best_lever: Design an experiment comparing compositionally and mechanically matched high-entropy alloy pairs that differ only in the ability to form a protective passivation layer under mechanical stress, quantifying simultaneous wear and corrosion rates.

families.principle: Integrating controlled experiments with simulation to iteratively validate and refine a unified mechanistic hypothesis, ensuring that predictions align with observations across scales.
cues_for: prior attempts separately investigated wear and corrosion
cues_against: The complexity of linking quantitative simulation data with experimental metrics may be challenging, although the question hints towards this integration
families.best_lever: Implement an iterative study where controlled variable experiments on high-entropy alloys inform mesoscale simulations of wear–corrosion processes, comparing predicted degradation phases with experimental baselines to validate the mechanism.

families.principle: Real-time observation of microstructural changes under combined mechanical and corrosive loading, providing direct evidence of mechanochemical coupling phenomena.
cues_against: The question stresses a controlled, matched comparison rather than solely observational insights
families.best_lever: Employ in-situ high-resolution microscopy (e.g., synchrotron X-ray or electron microscopy) during wear–corrosion tests to capture the initiation and degradation of protective films in real time.

families.principle: Using computational models to capture the mechanistic details of atomic- or mesoscale phenomena that govern the formation and breakdown of protective phases under combined degradation conditions.
cues_against: The question emphasizes a controlled experimental comparison and identification of regimes where predictions hold or fail, which is less directly provided by simulation alone
families.best_lever: Conduct reactive molecular dynamics or phase-field simulations that model the evolution of passivation layers under simultaneous mechanical stress and corrosive attack, highlighting pivotal atomic-scale events.

decision.trend: Initial HEA research largely investigated mechanical strength or corrosion resistance in isolation, with early studies emphasizing microstructural design and phase stability. Later, experiments began to probe the combined degradation behavior—most notably through tribocorrosion studies (PMC10456374) where the formation of a dense oxide layer (e.g., ZrTiO4) was correlated with improved wear-corrosion performance. Parallel work (PMC12565319) explored how compositional tuning could influence the development and stability of passive films. More recent investigations (PMC11169556) have provided mechanistic details on oxide growth and species distributions, yet these approaches have not yet unified the role of oxide film integrity and self-healing in resisting simultaneous wear and corrosion.
decision.unsolved: A singular, mechanistic hypothesis is still missing that explicitly links the integrity and self-healing of passive oxide films to the synergistic resistance against simultaneous mechanical wear and chemical corrosion. In particular, there is an unresolved need to decouple and quantitatively correlate the contributions of mechanical disruption and electrochemical degradation of the passive film under harsh conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled post‐processing thermal treatment (e.g., varying annealing temperature/time) to systematically modify the microstructure, thickness, and self-healing kinetics of the as-formed passive oxide film without changing the base alloy composition
decision.why: This lever directly targets the passive film—the root cause identified in the gap—by modulating its characteristics in a controlled manner. It follows from the trend where recent studies have linked oxide film integrity to improved tribocorrosion performance but have not isolated this mechanism. By comparing a baseline HEA with a thermally pre-treated variant under identical combined wear-corrosion tests, researchers can decouple the oxide film’s response from bulk alloy properties and validate whether enhanced self-healing indeed governs superior resistance.
